entity.name: Ibn Battuta
entity.description: The man who out-traveled Marco Polo threefold. A Moroccan legal scholar who left home at 21 for a pilgrimage and didn't return for 24 years, covering 117,000 km across Africa, Asia, and Europe. His travelogue, the Rihla, remains one of the most detailed accounts of the medieval world.

story.name: Ibn Battuta
story.description: A 21-year-old leaves Tangier alone for Mecca, visits Mogadishu at its zenith, reaches Delhi's sultan, and crosses the Sahara. The medieval world's greatest traveler, mapped across 117,000 km.

moments.name: A 21-Year-Old Scholar Leaves Tangier Alone for Mecca
moments.subtitle: He won't return home for 24 years or see his parents alive again
moments.description: On June 14, 1325, a 21-year-old Moroccan legal scholar named Ibn Battuta departed Tangier alone to perform the hajj pilgrimage to Mecca. Without companions or a caravan, driven by what he called an overmastering impulse, Ibn Battuta set out on a journey that would ordinarily take sixteen months. Instead, it became a 30-year odyssey covering 117,000 km across three continents, making him the most-traveled person in pre-modern history. Both his parents would die before his return.

moments.name: Ibn Battuta Completes His First Hajj Pilgrimage to Mecca
moments.subtitle: Rather than going home, the young scholar decides to keep traveling
moments.description: In November 1325, after traveling overland across North Africa and through Damascus, Ibn Battuta arrived in Mecca and completed his first hajj pilgrimage, earning the honorific El-Hajji. The journey had already taken him through Tlemcen, Tunis, Alexandria, and Cairo. Rather than returning to Morocco, Ibn Battuta chose to continue east toward the Ilkhanate, a Mongol khanate in Persia. This decision transformed a religious obligation into one of history's great voyages of discovery. He would eventually complete the hajj multiple times.

moments.name: Ibn Battuta Arrives in Mogadishu at the Zenith of Its Prosperity
moments.subtitle: The traveler describes a thriving Somali trading city exporting fabric to Egypt
moments.description: In 1332, Ibn Battuta arrived by ship in Mogadishu, then the pre-eminent city on the Horn of Africa. He described it as an exceedingly large city ruled by a Somali sultan, Abu Bakr ibn Shaikh Umar, who spoke both Somali and Arabic fluently. Ibn Battuta noted the city's many rich merchants and its high-quality fabric exports reaching as far as Egypt. His account provides one of the most detailed medieval descriptions of East African urban life, documenting a prosperous Swahili coast trading network that connected Africa, Arabia, and India.

moments.name: Ibn Battuta Reaches Kilwa, the Indian Ocean's Gold Trading Hub
moments.subtitle: A coral-stone mosque and royal palace mark the island's wealth
moments.description: Around 1330, Ibn Battuta sailed south along the Swahili coast and arrived in the island town of Kilwa in present-day Tanzania, a major transit center for the gold trade. He called it one of the finest and most beautifully built towns, noting its wooden buildings with reed roofs. Ibn Battuta praised the humility of Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman and described the Great Mosque of Kilwa, built of coral stones and the largest of its kind. His account remains a key primary source for understanding medieval East African trade networks that linked the interior gold mines to Indian Ocean commerce.

moments.name: Ibn Battuta Dictates His 30-Year Travel Memoir in Fez
moments.subtitle: A scholar named Ibn Juzayy transcribes 117,000 km of journeys into a single book
moments.description: Near the end of his life, Ibn Battuta settled in Morocco and dictated the account of his 30 years of travel to the scholar Ibn Juzayy. The resulting work, titled A Gift to Those Who Contemplate the Wonders of Cities and the Marvels of Travelling, became known simply as the Rihla. It documented Ibn Battuta's visits across Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia, India, Southeast Asia, and China, totaling roughly 117,000 km. The Rihla surpassed the accounts of Marco Polo and Zheng He as the most extensive pre-modern travel narrative ever composed.
